title: The Investing Fascia–Carotid Sheath Mechanistic Hypothesis of Internal Jugular Vein Outflow Obstruction
content: The clinical association between internal jugular vein (IJV) outflow obstruction and symptoms such as headache, pulsatile tinnitus, and cognitive decline has been repeatedly observed; however, “venous compression” alone is insufficient to explain the marked clinical heterogeneity of the condition. Among 283 patients with nonthrombotic IJV stenosis, the prevalence of headache was 65.02%; however, within the framework of this hypothesis, risk depends more on whether collateral compensatory capacity (and concurrent valvular antireflux function) is adequate than on the anatomical severity of stenosis—severe vertebral vein dilation, as a marker of adequate collateral compensation, was independently inversely associated with headache risk (OR = 0.184, 95% CI 0.092–0.366). Clinical consequences depend more on whether collateral compensation and valvular function remain sufficient to maintain outflow after compression. This hypothesis attributes this difference to whether compensation is adequate when IJV outflow is obstructed and proposes its upstream factor: sclerotic fibrosis of the investing fascia. Core proposition: Fibrosis of the investing fascia, through loss of elastic buffering and transmission of abnormal mechanical stress via the deep cervical fascial network to the carotid sheath, reduces collateral compensatory capacity when IJV outflow is obstructed and may coexist with insufficient valvular antireflux function; this state of inadequate compensation—centered on collateral compensation with valvular function as a parallel dimension—rather than luminal stenosis itself, is the key mediator linking extrasheath fascial pathology to fluctuating elevation of intracranial venous pressure. This framework provides a unified upstream mechanical perspective for understanding diseases and clinical phenotypes that share a common component of venous outflow obstruction, including headache associated with IJV stenosis, pulsatile tinnitus and cerebral tinnitus, exertional headache, Ménière disease, transient monocular blindness, insomnia, autonomic dysfunction, anxiety/depression/brain fog, vertigo, facial pain, and Eagle jugular syndrome. The hypothesis predicts that investing fascial stiffness is independently associated with compensatory indicators during IJV outflow obstruction; collateral compensatory capacity modifies the association between investing fascial fibrosis and symptoms; and relief of extrasheath mechanical constraint produces paired improvements in venous flow parameters and symptoms.
